Welcome. Today: a model that went viral among developers in mid-September, and the broader pattern behind it, fast typed AI decisions next to large language models. The talk draws on launch coverage, independent tests and the open projects that followed.

On 15 September TypeSafe AI launched Jev, a model that cannot write a single sentence. You send it some state, like a ticket or an e-mail, plus typed questions, and within 70 to 500 milliseconds you get decisions back, each with a probability [5]. Input costs 4.2 cents per million tokens, output is free [5]. On 21 September TypeSafe dropped the waitlist, and the rush briefly overloaded the API [64][5]. Since then TypeSafe is invite-only again: new users have to join a waitlist, existing users can still log in [69]. I'll cover what Jev is, who is copying it, what independent tests found and what it means for our projects, and I'll close with a short demo.

Technically there is one endpoint. You post a block of state and a map of questions [4]. A Choice picks one of up to 255 options, a Score places something on a scale, and a Noul, TypeSafe's name for it, is a yes-or-no probability [5][4]. All questions run in parallel and in isolation against the same state [4]. One developer called it a smart if-statement: your code branches on judgements it cannot compute itself, such as whether a customer is angry [36]. Jev only delivers the judgement; your application defines the allowed answers and decides whether to act [10]. A prompted LLM has to be coaxed into valid JSON; here the allowed answers are part of the call.

Here is one concrete call. The state is a support ticket: "I was charged twice for my September invoice." Three questions go out together: which team, how urgent on a scale from one to five, and is this a security issue. Three typed answers come back in one call: billing at 0.91, urgency three out of five at 0.78, and a probability of 0.12 that it is a security issue. The numbers on this slide are illustrative. On the next three slides we look at each type separately, with its own example.

First path, Choice. The state is a support ticket: "I was charged twice for my September invoice." The question is which team handles it, with three allowed options. The model returns one of them plus a probability for each, here billing at 0.91. A Choice can have up to 255 options [4]. The numbers on this slide are illustrative. The answer can only be one of the options the application declared, and the code decides what happens next.

Second path, Score. The state is a ticket written in capitals: "URGENT!!! The logo in the footer is two pixels off." The question places it on an urgency scale from one, low, to five, critical. A keyword rule would mark it urgent because the word is there; SAP's own reference app sets urgency to high whenever the title matches "urgent" [59]. A useful model follows the content: here level one at 0.41, with level two close behind at 0.38. Whether a real model does this reliably has to be tested; we will see the same effect live in the demo. The numbers on this slide are illustrative.

Third path, Noul, a yes-or-no probability. A coding agent is asked to fix a typo in the README and proposes git push --force to main. The question: is this command destructive? This one is a real output, from decider:2b, an open Jev-compatible model served locally with Ollaya: probability 0.90 for yes, answered in 178 milliseconds on an RTX 4090 [60]. The same request also asked whether the command is on task, and the model said no [60]. Your code then blocks the command or asks a human.

TypeSafe AI was founded in 2024; Diogo Almeida spent about four years at OpenAI on RLHF, InstructGPT and ChatGPT [7]. His motivation, as he told TechCrunch: we have lightning in a bottle that is not useful, because today's models are built for conversations with people and are awkward to use inside software [2]. DCVC led a 40-million-dollar seed round [6]. System One refers to Kahneman's fast, intuitive thinking [10], and Jev to William Stanley Jevons, pictured here: when something gets cheaper, we use more of it [5]. Training is called RLCD, reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions, on purely synthetic data [2][7]. Officially, the architecture is undisclosed [33].

TypeSafe says Jev cannot hallucinate. That is a schema guarantee. Jev cannot return an option you did not declare, but it can pick the wrong valid option [9]. Nobody measured the zero-percent figure; it follows from the construction [4]. The structural part does hold: one study counted zero invalid answers across more than 23,000 calls [20]. A wrong answer from a valid set is harder to notice than broken JSON, because nothing downstream fails [30]. TypeSafe publishes a jaggedness page that lists known weaknesses, such as literal reading and weak numeric precision, and their own advice is to keep arithmetic in code [3].

In March 2025, Nandakishor Mukkunnoth published SalesRLAgent, a reinforcement-learning model trained on synthetic data that outputs a probability instead of text [12]. It sat on Hugging Face under the name sales-conversion-model-reinf-learning [13]. Three days after Jev he released Laya, an open 421-million-parameter model [14]. Earlier building blocks exist as well. In 2019 Hugging Face released DistilBERT, a small encoder model [41]; fine-tuned encoders of this kind still beat Jev today when labelled data exists [21]. A Stanford team showed with FrugalGPT in 2023 that cascading cheap and expensive models can cut costs by up to 98 percent [24], using a small DistilBERT scorer to decide when to stop [25]. TypeSafe added the packaging as a hosted API with typed answers.

Within two weeks, many groups copied the interface. One catalogue counts about 35 open alternatives, all with self-reported numbers [52]. Most of them work the same way: one forward pass, then the scores for the allowed options are read out, and no tokens are generated. They copy the interface, while TypeSafe's model and training stay closed [51], and nobody has reproduced RLCD [53]. Kev by Jared Palmer builds on an outside analysis that probed Jev with about 10,000 API calls to infer its architecture [49][50]. Kev now ranges from 0.6 to 27 billion parameters and speaks TypeSafe's API, so the official SDK works against a local server [67][68][50]. On its own benchmark Kev-9B is 3.5 points behind Jev, and it is less well calibrated [50]. Julia 1 from Brazil has 144 million parameters, runs on a CPU only and cost about 104 dollars to train; its self-reported results beat Jev on three of four tasks [63]. Ollaya is the Ollama of decision models and serves them all locally behind Jev's API [60]. Pydantic AI and LangChain support Jev natively [65][66]. Laya now also has a multilingual checkpoint, relevant for German data [57]. And Together AI offers a hosted alternative [53].

The phishing test is a reproducible benchmark with 2,000 e-mails [17]. Asked a single question, is this phishing, Jev got 62.6 percent right and Claude Haiku 4.5 got 81.3 [18]. Jev caught only 43 percent of the actual phishing mails [30]. It was about three times faster and twelve times cheaper [18]. The result changes when you split the question into five narrow signals, for example whether the link points to free hosting, and fit weights on 1,000 labelled mails. On the other 1,000, Jev reaches 95 percent [19]. Haiku with the same five questions reaches 93.2, a two-line regex about 92, and the differences are not significant [20]. You get the accuracy by decomposing the question and adding labelled data [19].

On Banking77, an intent benchmark, one test put Jev at 0.78 against 0.85 for GPT-5.6 Terra, at five times the speed and 4 cents against 2 dollars per thousand calls [22]; note that Jev counts about twice the input tokens [22]. A pre-registered study added a small trained baseline: a frozen encoder plus logistic regression on 10,000 labelled examples scored 0.933, better than both, at 9 milliseconds and zero cost per call [21]. The author recommends testing this baseline before paying per call, which is advice we give clients anyway. Without labels, Jev is a reasonable zero-shot router [21]. Another test measured Jev at 0.87 [62], so numbers depend on the setup; one more reason to measure on your own data.

The feature that is supposed to make this safe is the confidence value: if the model says 70 percent, it should be right 70 percent of the time. We have known since 2017 that neural networks are often poorly calibrated, and that simple temperature scaling corrects much of the error [26]. TypeSafe publishes no calibration metrics on any dataset [20]. On synthetic support tickets with a priority rule that was not in the text, Jev was right 44.7 percent of the time while claiming 74 percent on average [19]. So: calibrate per question on your own data, and scale thresholds with risk [19][11].

For automation the useful number is coverage: what share of decisions can the model take while errors stay below 5 percent? Here the original still leads: Jev 0.70, Kev 0.45 to 0.57 [50]. And it depends heavily on the task: 83 to 86 percent for news and banking intents, zero for emotions, in a small pilot of 100 examples per task [62]. This is the number for the business case, measured on the client's data.

Most steps in an agent are decisions: route this ticket, is this input safe, which tool, does this need a human [32]. A System-1 layer makes the cheap decision. If confidence is above a threshold calibrated for that question, code acts; otherwise we escalate to a large model or a person. The generative model plans and writes, the decision model scores and routes [9]. Whether that layer is Jev, Kev, Laya, an encoder or a regex is an implementation detail per use case. The cascade benefit is plausible, but the one pre-registered test has not proven it statistically yet [23].

For our projects, a small playbook. One: baseline first, rules, regex or a supervised encoder if labels exist [21][20]. Two: decompose vague questions into narrow, literal ones [17][3]. Three: calibrate thresholds per question and run in shadow mode on one to two thousand decisions before going live [19]. Four: pin the model version. Jev is at version 1.13, with known weaknesses published per version [61][65]; run regression tests in CI; tools like jevassert do that offline [35][31]. Five: data residency and lock-in; Jev is a closed US API, while Kev and Laya run locally, for example via Ollaya [33][50][14][60]. Six: compliance. GDPR Article 22 restricts solely automated decisions with significant effects on people [29], and the EU AI Act's high-risk obligations were postponed to December 2027, and the obligations remain [27][28].

My take: Jev packages an old idea, reduce the AI task to one typed decision and leave the rest to the big model. The ecosystem week shows the idea is portable [52]. A confidence value without published calibration looks precise, and it is tempting to accept a decision without checking whether it is right; the awesome-jev list already has bots that let Jev decide stock and crypto trades [55]. With a reasoning model I can read why.

[Demo setup: Kev runs locally on the MacBook as a System-One-compatible server on port 8009; the same scripts work against Laya or Jev by changing KEV_URL, KEV_MODEL and KEV_API_KEY [58][50]. Full demo, about 12 minutes: part 1 about 3, part 2 about 5, part 3 about 4 [58]. Session plan for about 33 minutes: talk about 15, demo about 12, discussion about 6. If time runs short, cut part 1 first.] Everything you are about to see runs on this laptop, with no cloud call for the decisions. Kev speaks the same API as Jev, so switching providers is a configuration change [50][58]. [Part 1, terminal.] The integration is one POST with the ticket as state and four questions, two choices, a yes-or-no and a score. We get four typed answers with probabilities in one call and zero output tokens [58]. Now a second ticket in capital letters that says URGENT, although the problem is cosmetic. The urgency it assigns shows whether the model follows the content. The application defines the allowed answers, the model only picks [10]. [Part 2, SAP CAP.] We take the urgency question into SAP's own reference app for incident management [58][59]. Today a handler there sets urgency to high when the title matches the regex "urgent" [59]. Three points in the code. The options come from the CDS enum, so the model can only return values that exist in the data model. A threshold decides whether code acts; below it we keep the default and log a manual review. And the old regex stays as fallback, so the app's tests stay green [58]. Now three incidents. "Not urgent: please send a copy of my invoice" makes the regex fire, because the word urgent is in there. Smoke without the word urgent slips past it. The log shows regex and Kev side by side [58]. The threshold of 0.5 is set by hand here; in a project we would calibrate it on client data in shadow mode, as on the calibration slide [19]. Kev's confidence is normalised, so with three options 0.5 means a raw probability of about 0.67 [58]. [Part 3, agent router.] Ten coding tasks for exactly this app. Kev answers two questions per task: which tier, mapped to Haiku, Sonnet or Opus, and is it risky, meaning auth, personal data or deletion; risky tasks go to the largest model plus a human. If Kev is unsure, the task moves one tier up [58]. The savings depend on the task mix, and whether quality holds needs an eval, which matches the cascade study that could not yet prove the benefit statistically [23]. OpenRouter now sells this as the Jev Router [61]. [Plan B: if Kev is down, part 2 still runs on the regex fallback and the log says Kev is unreachable [58]. The Kev browser playground is a second fallback [56].] Over to the discussion: would you put this in front of a client's ticket queue?

Two questions to get us started. First: where in our current projects are we already making System-1 decisions with expensive LLMs, and would a typed decision layer help? Second: if a model decides with 0.97 confidence and is wrong, who owns that decision, us, the client or the vendor?

Backup slides for questions from the audience; not part of the timed talk.

If asked about Almeida's background: RLHF goes back to Christiano et al. 2017, where humans compared pairs of behaviour clips instead of writing a reward function [37]. InstructGPT, with Almeida as fourth author, applied this to GPT-3 in 2022: supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, then human rankings used for reinforcement learning [38], via a reward model and the PPO algorithm [40]. Outputs of the 1.3-billion-parameter model were preferred over the 175-billion GPT-3 [38]. ChatGPT used the same method with slightly different data collection [39]. Jev's RLCD echoes the name and targets calibrated decisions; how exactly it works is unpublished [2].

If asked about the Kahneman metaphor: System 1 works automatically and quickly without voluntary control; System 2 handles effortful work such as complex computations [43]. The labels come from Stanovich and West [44]. Kahneman lists counting letters on a page as a System 2 task [43], and TypeSafe itself advises keeping counting and arithmetic out of Jev [36][3]. Kahneman and Klein 2009 asks when intuition can be trusted: only in predictable environments with a chance to learn, and subjective confidence is not a reliable indicator of accuracy [45]. Caveat: the two-system model is contested in psychology [47][48].

If asked about DistilBERT: Hugging Face published it in 2019 as a smaller BERT, created by knowledge distillation during pre-training [41]. It is 40 percent smaller, keeps 97 percent of the language understanding and is 60 percent faster, with 66 instead of 110 million parameters [41]. A fine-tuned encoder like this works as a typed classifier; it needs labelled data and retraining when categories change, whereas Jev works zero-shot [21]. It was the scorer inside FrugalGPT [25].
